hook.situation: You arrive at a restaurant in Seoul. The host asks '예약이 있으세요?' (Do you have a reservation?) — you freeze. You know 있어요 means something like 'there is' or 'have', but why does 예약이 have that 이 on it? And how do you say you DON'T have one? This chapter gives you the two sentences that unlock dozens of real situations.
objectives: Use 있어요 and 없어요 to express existence ('there is / there isn't') and possession ('I have / I don't have')
Attach the subject particle 이/가 correctly to the noun that exists or is possessed
Avoid the #1 beginner error: using 을/를 (object marker) instead of 이/가 with 있어요/없어요
hook.whyItMatters: 있어요 and 없어요 are two of the most-used words in Korean. They cover 'is there a bathroom?', 'do you have time?', 'no problem', 'no money' — the building blocks of travel, small talk, and daily life. The subject particle 이/가 that comes with them is equally essential: nearly every Korean sentence uses it. Master these now and half of Chapter 5 and 6 becomes review.

grammarNotes.title: 있어요 / 없어요 — Existence and Possession
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 있어요 as a PRESENCE LAMP and 없어요 as the lamp being OFF. The noun before 이/가 is the thing you're checking: is the lamp on or off for this noun? 시간이 있어요 — is time present? Lamp ON. 시간이 없어요 — lamp OFF. One switch, two possible states, any noun you like.
grammarNotes.formation:
[Noun]이/가 있어요 → [Noun] exists / I have [Noun]
[Noun]이/가 없어요 → [Noun] doesn't exist / I don't have [Noun]

이 after a final consonant (시간이, 문제가 → wait, 문제 ends in a vowel so → 문제가)
가 after a final vowel (친구가, 예약이 → 예약 ends in ㄱ so → 예약이)

examples.note: 시간 ends in consonant ㄴ → subject particle 이. The question asks if the 'presence lamp' for time is on.
예약 ends in consonant ㄱ → particle 이. This sentence doubles as 'there is a reservation' depending on context.
돈 ends in consonant ㄴ → particle 이. Lamp is OFF for money.
문제 ends in vowel 에 → particle 가. A very natural reassurance phrase.
화장실 ends in consonant ㄹ → particle 이. One of the most essential travel questions.

contrastPairs.explanation: The noun (시간이) and particle stay exactly the same — only the verb flips between 있어요 (present) and 없어요 (absent). Swapping the verb is all you need to move from yes to no.
Same structure, same particle 이, opposite meaning. At a hotel or restaurant you'll use both — the first when you've planned ahead, the second when you're hoping for a walk-in.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: In English 'I have time' uses 'have' as a transitive verb with an object ('time'), so learners instinctively reach for the object marker 을/를. But 있어요 is NOT a transitive verb in Korean — it means 'exists' or 'is present.' The noun is the SUBJECT of existence, so it takes the subject particle 이/가. Never pair 있어요 or 없어요 with 을/를.

exceptions: 있다 can also mean 'to stay' or 'to remain' (as an action): 잠깐 있어요 — 'stay for a moment.' In that case no 이/가 is needed because there's no subject noun for existence.
In colloquial speech the subject 이/가 is often dropped when context is clear: '있어요?' (Do you have it?) with no noun is natural when the topic has already been mentioned.
제가 (not 저가) is the irregular form of 저 + 가: 제가 없어요 (I don't have it). This is the one common irregular with 가.

grammarNotes.title: 이 / 가 — The Subject Particle
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 이/가 as a SPOTLIGHT. It shines directly on one noun and says: 'This specific thing — right here — is the one that exists, hurts, appears, or matters right now.' When the spotlight hits a word, 이/가 is attached. 이 goes after a dark (consonant-ending) sound; 가 goes after a bright (vowel-ending) sound.
grammarNotes.formation:
Noun ending in consonant + 이: 시간이, 화장실이, 예약이
Noun ending in vowel + 가: 친구가, 문제가, 커피가

Special: 나 → 내가, 저 → 제가 (irregular, must be memorized)

examples.en: I have a friend. / A friend is here.
examples.note: 친구 ends in vowel 구 → particle 가. The spotlight is on 친구 — that's the thing that exists.
머리 ends in vowel 리 → particle 가. The spotlight is on 머리 as the thing experiencing pain.
누구 + 가 = 누가 (contracted). The spotlight asks: which person specifically appeared?
저 + 가 = 제가 (irregular). Spotlight on 'I' as the subject — used when introducing yourself or clarifying who does the action.
비 ends in vowel → 가. 비가 와요 is a set phrase — the spotlight identifies rain as the thing arriving.

a.en: As for me, I'm a student. (topic — background info)

b.en: I am the student. (subject — specific, important)

contrastPairs.explanation: 은/는 sets the topic — it's like a soft background frame. 이/가 puts a spotlight on the noun — it's highlighting or specifying. When answering '누가 학생이에요?' (Who is the student?), you must say 제가 학생이에요, not 저는.

a.en: Coffee is good. (general opinion about coffee as a topic)

b.en: I like coffee. / Coffee is the good thing. (spotlight on coffee as the object of liking)

contrastPairs.explanation: 좋아요 (to like, to be good) uses 이/가 for the thing liked: N이/가 좋아요. Using 은/는 instead shifts it to a general statement about a topic. Both are grammatically possible but carry subtly different meaning.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 저 (polite 'I') contracts with 가 to form 제가 — this is an irregular form that must be memorized. Saying 저가 is not natural Korean. Similarly, 나 + 가 = 내가 in casual speech. These two pronouns are the only common irregulars with 이/가.

exceptions: 나 → 내가 (casual I + subject), 저 → 제가 (polite I + subject) — both are contractions, not the regular rule
누구 → 누가 when asking 'who' as a subject: 누가 왔어요? (not 누구가)
이/가 is often omitted in casual speech when the subject is obvious from context — this is normal and natural, not a mistake

exampleSentence.en: Do you have time right now?
exampleSentence.note: 시간 ends in consonant ㄴ → 시간이. The presence lamp: is time available?
예약 ends in consonant ㄱ → 예약이. Essential phrase at hotels and restaurants.

exampleSentence.en: I don't have money right now.
exampleSentence.note: 돈 ends in consonant ㄴ → 돈이. A survival phrase for daily life.
문제 ends in vowel 에 → 문제가. A very common reassurance phrase.
화장실 ends in consonant ㄹ → 화장실이. One of the most important travel questions.
친구 ends in vowel 구 → 친구가. Spotlight on the friend as the one who exists/is present.
방 ends in consonant ㅇ → 방이. Essential hotel check-in phrase.
자리 ends in vowel 리 → 자리가. Used at restaurants, cafés, cinemas.
물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 물이. Works for 'there is no water' or 'I don't have water.'
시간이 있다 is the go-to way to ask if someone is available — more natural than direct schedule questions.

collocations: 시간이 있을 때 (when you have time)

exampleSentence.en: There is milk in the fridge.
exampleSentence.note: 있어요 checks the presence lamp: is milk in the fridge? Yes. Note 에 for the location and 이/가 for the thing that exists.

collocations: N에 있어요 (something IS at a place)

exampleSentence.note: 없어요 is the lamp-OFF version. 오늘은 sets the time as topic with 은/는; 시간이 is the subject of non-existence.

exampleSentence.en: There are a lot of people today.
exampleSentence.note: 사람이 많아요 uses 이/가 — the spotlight is on 사람 as the thing that is plentiful. 많다 often pairs with 이/가.
When 예약 is used as a verb (예약하다), the restaurant is the object → 을/를. Compare: 예약이 있어요 (the reservation exists → 이/가).

extendedVocabulary.english: to hurt / be sick / be in pain

exampleSentence.note: 배 ends in vowel 배 → 배가. The body part that hurts takes 이/가 — this is a core pattern for describing symptoms.

exampleSentence.en: I like coffee. / Coffee is good.
exampleSentence.note: In the 'I like X' pattern, X takes 이/가, not 을/를. The spotlight (이/가) is on the thing liked, not the object of an action.

extendedDialogue.setting: Minji and Junho are checking in at a hotel in Busan

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Welcome. Do you have a reservation?
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 있으세요? — 예약 ends in ㄱ → 이. 있으세요 is the honorific form of 있어요, used to a customer.

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: Yes, I have a reservation. I booked it under Minji.
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 있어요 — presence lamp ON for the reservation. 민지로 = 'under (the name) Minji' (로 = direction/means).

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Just a moment... I'm sorry, there is no reservation.
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 없어요 — same noun + particle, opposite verb. Lamp OFF. The contrast shows how the same frame flips with 있어요/없어요.

lines.speaker: 준호
lines.en: Hey, there's a problem! I definitely made a reservation.
lines.grammarNote: 문제가 있어요 — 문제 ends in vowel 에 → 가. Notice 문제가 있어요 (there IS a problem) vs. 문제가 없어요 (no problem).

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.ko: 다시 확인할게요. 혹시 빈 방이 있어요.
lines.romanization: Dasi hwaginhalgeyo. Hoksi bin bangi isseoyo.
lines.en: Let me check again. There is a vacant room available.
lines.grammarNote: 방이 있어요 — 방 ends in consonant ㅇ → 이. 빈 방 = vacant room (빈 is an adjective modifying 방).

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.grammarNote: 자리가 있어요 — 자리 ends in vowel 리 → 가. Here 자리 means 'spot/room available' in a broader sense.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.romanization: Ne, i-cheunge bangi isseoyo. Munjega eopseoyo.
lines.en: Yes, there's a room on the 2nd floor. No problem.
lines.grammarNote: 방이 있어요 (room exists → 이/가) + 에 for location on the floor. 문제가 없어요 = classic reassurance phrase.

lines.speaker: 준호
lines.en: Thank you! And is there a bathroom?
lines.grammarNote: 화장실이 있어요? — 화장실 ends in consonant ㄹ → 이. The question form of 있어요 is simply 있어요 with rising intonation.

readingText.title: 호텔 예약 문자 (Hotel Booking Text Exchange)
readingText.body:
유나: 오빠, 내일 시간이 있어요?
준서: 네, 시간이 있어요. 왜요?
유나: 부산에 같이 가요! 호텔 예약이 있어요?
준서: 아직 예약이 없어요. 지금 바로 예약할게요.
유나: 빈 방이 있어요?
준서: 네, 바다 뷰 방이 있어요. 문제가 없어요!
유나: 완전 좋아요! 돈이 있어요?
준서: 네, 돈이 있어요. 걱정하지 마세요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Yuna: Oppa, do you have time tomorrow?
Junseo: Yes, I have time. Why?
Yuna: Let's go to Busan together! Do you have a hotel reservation?
Junseo: Not yet, there's no reservation. I'll book it right now.
Yuna: Is there a vacant room?
Junseo: Yes, there's a room with an ocean view. No problem!
Yuna: That's great! Do you have money?
Junseo: Yes, I have money. Don't worry.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Does Junseo already have a hotel reservation when the conversation starts?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: No. He says 아직 예약이 없어요 (Not yet, there is no reservation). He books one during the conversation.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What kind of room does Junseo find?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바다 뷰 방 — a room with an ocean view.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 이/가 있어요 or 이/가 없어요 in the text. For each, identify the noun, explain why 이 or 가 was chosen, and state whether it expresses existence or possession.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 1) 시간이 있어요 (×2) — 시간 ends in ㄴ → 이; possession (I have time). 2) 예약이 있어요 — 예약 ends in ㄱ → 이; possession (has a reservation). 3) 예약이 없어요 — same noun + particle, reversed meaning; absence. 4) 방이 있어요 — 방 ends in ㅇ → 이; existence (a room exists). 5) 문제가 없어요 — 문제 ends in vowel 에 → 가; absence (no problem). 6) 돈이 있어요 — 돈 ends in ㄴ → 이; possession (has money). Pattern: every time, the particle choice follows the consonant/vowel rule — not the meaning.

culturalNote.title: 문제가 없어요 — The Korean 'No Problem'
culturalNote.body: You'll hear 문제가 없어요 constantly in Korean service situations — at hotels, restaurants, customer service lines, and repair shops. It functions just like 'no problem' or 'all good' in English, and it always brings a sense of relief. The reverse, 문제가 있어요, is softer than it sounds: Koreans tend to say it matter-of-factly rather than dramatically. A related phrase you'll encounter is 괜찮아요 (it's okay / I'm fine), which overlaps in meaning. But when a Korean staff member says 문제가 없어요 after checking something for you, you can relax — that's their professional 'everything checks out.'

inlineExercises.explanation: 시간 ends in consonant ㄴ → subject particle 이. You cannot use 을 (object marker) with 있어요 — that is the most common beginner mistake. 가 would be wrong here because 가 attaches after vowels only.
문제 ends in vowel 에 → subject particle 가. 이 would be wrong because 이 only follows consonant-final nouns. 를 (object marker) is never used with 없어요 — absence is not an action performed on an object.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '예약을 없어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 없어요 means 'does not exist / do not have' — the noun is the SUBJECT of non-existence, so it needs the subject particle 이/가, not the object marker 을/를. 예약 ends in consonant ㄱ → 예약이.

inlineExercises.hint: 화장실 ends in a consonant. Which particle follows a consonant-final noun? The question form of 있어요 uses rising intonation — the word order stays the same.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I like coffee.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 좋아요 (to be good/to like) uses 이/가, not 을/를. The thing you like is the subject of being-good, so it takes the subject spotlight particle 이/가. 커피를 좋아요 is ungrammatical. 커피는 좋아요 is possible but shifts meaning to a general topic statement ('Coffee, in general, is good') rather than expressing personal preference.
배 ends in vowel 배 → particle 가. The body part that hurts takes 이/가 in Korean — this is the same spotlight pattern as with 있어요/없어요. Never use 을 for a body part with 아프다.

inlineExercises.prompt: The hotel receptionist has found your reservation. Which sentence would they say?
inlineExercises.explanation: 예약이 있어요 — reservation exists → lamp ON → correct. 예약이 없어요 is the opposite (no reservation found). 예약을 있어요 is ungrammatical — 있어요 can never take 을/를.

bullets: PRESENCE LAMP: 있어요 = lamp ON (exists / have), 없어요 = lamp OFF (doesn't exist / don't have)
SPOTLIGHT particle 이/가: attaches to the noun that exists — 이 after consonant (시간이, 예약이), 가 after vowel (문제가, 친구가)
Never use 을/를 with 있어요 or 없어요 — the thing that exists is a SUBJECT, not an object
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 5 introduces daily action verbs and 을/를 (object markers) — now you'll finally get to use 을/를, but with action verbs like 먹다 and 마시다, not with 있어요/없어요.
